notes.1ai: Most candidates measured and recorded the unstretched length of the spring and also recorded it in the appropriate place in the table. The instruction to record the length in centimetres to the nearest millimetre was usually followed. However, sometimes the length of the spring was recorded to the nearest centimetre and sometimes, even to 0.01 cm.
notes.1aii: Candidates were then required to draw a diagram of the spring to clearly show the length that they had measured. There was much evidence to suggest that many candidates did not read the question carefully. These candidates tried to show how to measure the length, drawing rulers and set squares, rather than just doing as asked, and showing the length that they had measured, e.g. with a line or an arrow on a sketch of the spring. Many candidates spent time drawing the detailed set-up but then failed to identify the actual length that needed to be measured.
notes.1b: The actual experiment was performed well, with most candidates completing the table to show the length of the spring as the load on the spring was varied. The calculation of the extensions produced by the loads was done well, but a number of candidates calculated incremental, rather than total extensions. Some candidates rounded their correctly calculated extensions to the nearest whole number. This was presumably to make the graph plotting exercise which followed easier. This is not good practice and candidates should be discouraged from doing this.
notes.1c: Graph-plotting skills were of a reasonable standard, but many responses failed to gain full credit. The most common sources of error were: • awkward scales, such as 3 or 7; choosing such scales makes the points much harder to plot • missing labels and/or units on the axes • choosing scales so that the plotted points did not cover at least half of the given grid • failure to plot the first point for which L = 0 and e = 0 • forcing the line of best fit to pass through the origin (whether plotted or not), resulting in an inappropriate line of best fit. There were, however, still many excellent, carefully drawn, best-fit lines produced by candidates.
notes.1d: Although most candidates gained full credit for this question, some candidates did not. Candidates were asked to indicate on the graph, how they obtained the information. This was often missing, as was the unit of their answer.
notes.2a: Room temperature was recorded by nearly every candidate.
notes.2b: The taking and recording of the temperature of the hot water as it cooled caused very few problems. A minority of candidates failed to let the thermometer reading reach its maximum value before starting to time the water cooling. There were also instances of over-precise temperatures being recorded. The instruction to complete the column headings in the table was very often missed by candidates.
notes.2ci: The calculation of the average rate of cooling of the water over the duration of the experiment was done well. There were occasional rounding errors and answers being left as fractions.
notes.2cii: A number of correctly calculated rates were rounded to just 1 significant figure.
notes.2d: Most candidates were able to give at least one change to the experiment that would increase the rate of cooling of the hot water, without changing the starting temperature of the water. The most common correct answers were to remove the lid or to use a wider surface area. Occasionally, suggestions did just the opposite of what was required, e.g. using a thicker lid or wrapping the beaker in insulation.
notes.2e: Many candidates misinterpreted what was required here, namely how accurate temperatures of the cooling water are obtained during the experiment. Creditworthy answers referred to perpendicular viewing of the thermometer scale, stirring the water before taking a reading, ensuring that the thermometer does not touch the sides of the beaker etc. Many responses were related to the accuracy of the final result or to improvements to the experiment. Answers such as repeat and average or keep the room temperature constant were common.
notes.3a: Most candidates followed the instructions, drew around the semicircular block on the ray-trace sheet, labelled the block and drew a normal through the centre of AB.
notes.3b: Not all candidates were able to locate and identify the refracted ray. Some of these rays were in the wrong quadrants, and some were obviously reflected and not refracted rays. Most candidates did not gain full credit because the pin separation they used was far too small.
notes.3c: It was usually possible to identify the angle that candidates were measuring.
notes.3d: Only stronger candidates were able to identify a precaution that needed to be taken to produce an accurate ray trace. Common incorrect answers were “view the pins at right angles”, “avoid parallax” and “keep one eye closed”. Answers such as “view the bases of the pins”, “ensure that the pins are vertical” and “draw thin lines” scored credit here.
notes.3e: Many candidates’ drawings contained rays in the wrong quadrant – presumably these had been refracted rather than totally internally reflected. If candidates had viewed the pins from the position of the eye in the diagram on the question paper, they would have had much greater success.
notes.3f: Candidates found this challenging and some did not seem to understand which angle to measure. The question was answered well by stronger candidates, but for many candidates, it was often difficult to determine which angle was being measured. Some candidates, drawing upon their knowledge of the laws of reflection, wrote down the correct answer of 70°, but the actual angle on their ray trace sheet was very different.
